notation.kind: Endogenous in a closed economy; exogenous here

blocks.md: A small open economy trades with the rest of the world but is too small for its own choices to move world prices. Think of a single farmer selling wheat in a global market: however much or little she grows, the price of wheat is set elsewhere. In the same way, a small country can sell as many planes or import as much cloth as it likes at the going world price. That makes life simple for an analyst: changes in world prices — from a trade deal, a tariff abroad or a new competitor — arrive from outside, and the question is only how the economy responds to them.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: Treating prices as given turns trade shocks into exogenous price changes, which is what lets simple models trace them to wages and incomes.
An economy whose demand and supply are negligible relative to world markets, so the prices of traded goods are exogenous to it:

blocks.tex: p_j = p_j^{W} \quad \text{for every traded good } j

blocks.md:
| | Small open economy | Large or closed economy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prices of traded goods | Given by world markets | Set by domestic supply and demand |
| Effect of its own tariff on world prices | None | Can improve its terms of trade |
| Domestic shocks | Change quantities traded, not prices | Change prices |
| Trade shocks | Arrive as exogenous price changes | Partly absorbed by price adjustments |

- Assuming non-traded goods (haircuts, housing) also have world prices — only traded goods do.
- Applying small-economy results to a large economy such as the US without checking whether its choices move world prices; models often make the assumption for tractability, not realism.

- Trade: specific-factors and Heckscher-Ohlin analysis of price shocks ([Specific-Factors Model](note:specific-factors-model)).
- Open-economy macro: a given world interest rate pins down capital flows.
